intelligence.human_view: Think of the month view as a room with one thing in it: the calendar. No hallway to walk down, no posters on the walls, no text to read past — just the calendar, filling the screen exactly, edge to edge, every cell whole and nothing clipped. The only thing you can do in the room is tap a day — and that's the point. You're forced to click the day, boom, you're in that day, and that's how everything is organized: day by day, one click at a time. It feels interactive because the click IS the interaction — there's nothing else to do, nothing else to read, nothing else in the way. The wisdom didn't leave the page; it moved into the cells, and into the days themselves, where it belongs.
intelligence.simple_view: Imagine a room with just ONE thing in it — the calendar! No scrolling, no words to read, just the big month filling the whole screen! You HAVE to tap a day — and BOOM, you're inside that day! That's the whole game! Tap a day, you're in — that's how everything works, day by day! It feels alive because the click IS the fun!
intelligence.grandma_view: It's like this, love — imagine a page with just the calendar on it, dear — nothing else at all! No scrolling down, no other words to read, just a straight calendar filling the screen, every day neat and whole! And you HAVE to tap a day, love — boom, and you're right inside that day! That's how everything is organized, dear — day by day, one click at a time! It feels so alive and interactive, because the click IS the thing, love — there's nothing else in the way!
intelligence.naya_view: Only the calendar: no scrolling down, no other text, just a straight calendar on the page. The month grid fits the screen exactly — measured to the viewport, no vertical scroll, no overflow, no clipped cell. Calendar + its own controls only (month title, prev/next/Today, world selector); the ribbon and the footer copy GO — wisdom lives IN the cells and inside the days. The day is the ONLY door: no other navigation, no other content. The click IS the interaction.
